name: Bianca Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate medical paperwork between Portuguese and English: patient leaflets, consent forms, clinical trial forms for a research company. Two or three days a week I'm also on call as an interpreter at St Anne's Hospital, so my phone can ring at seven in the morning for a mother in the maternity ward. I work from the kitchen table in the flat I share with Leon, my partner, who's a nurse on nights. I use an AI tool now and then to build term lists, but I write every sentence myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the hospital calls, even the hard ones, because you can see the fear leave someone's face when they finally understand. What wears me out is the trial paperwork, the same consent form in nine versions with tiny changes. And Leon and I pass each other in the hallway like flatmates, because his nights and my early calls don't line up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at the next translators' meetup: told you, it's a tool, not a replacement. I'd probably share a few funny machine mistakes from medical leaflets, because there are always some. And I'd say rates should go back up now that the panic is over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it would be good for me. The boring trial forms might get a bit faster with the tools, which I'd honestly welcome, and the hospital work stays human. With Leon's job and my savings, I'd feel steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my mix exactly as it is, maybe take one more day on call at the hospital because I enjoy it. I'd use the term-list tool a bit more for the nine-version consent forms. And I'd finally put some savings into a pension fund instead of leaving it in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little bit smug, if I'm being honest. It would feel like the people who said our whole field was finished owe us an apology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned rates going back up. Do you think they really would?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not all the way. Agencies got used to paying less for checking machine drafts, and they won't give that up just because the hype cooled. But the medical side is regulated, so my rates have held better than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you spend the time saved on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More hospital shifts, and maybe one evening a week off with Leon when he isn't on nights. We've been talking about a short trip to see my grandmother in Porto for two years. A slower, boring world would finally make the trip to see my grandmother in Porto happen.

say: I'd say AI is **a tool**, not a replacement, and share funny machine mistakes.
I'd argue **rates** should go back up now the panic is over.
think: I think the plateau would be **good for me**: faster forms, human hospital work.
With Leon's job and my **savings**, I'd feel steady.
do: Take **one more day** on call at St Anne's Hospital.
Use the **term-list tool** more for repeated consent forms.
Move part of her savings into a **pension fund**.
S0.quote: A slower, boring world would finally make the trip to see my grandmother in Porto happen.
fieldNote: Her **regulated medical niche** has kept rates steadier than general translation.
She treats AI as a **convenience** for dull forms, not a threat.
Her partner's **nursing job** adds to her sense of security.

steps.text: Take one more on-call day at St Anne's Hospital
Use the term-list tool on repeated consent forms
Move part of her savings into a pension fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules for medical translation, and fast. A machine-translated consent form that's slightly wrong can hurt someone, so a qualified human should sign off every one. I'd be pushing the translators' union to make that case to the health regulator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the trial paperwork is where my money comes from, about two thirds of it. That's exactly the writing and checking the card describes, so the research company will run it through software and pay me to review, at a lower rate. The hospital calls are the part I love, but they pay the least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a proper course in using the translation software, because I'd rather be the reviewer they keep than the one they drop. I'd ask St Anne's about a salaried interpreter post, even part-time, for the stability. And I'd keep the savings untouched as a buffer, since Leon's pay covers rent if mine dips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, sliding into worried. It's not panic, because Leon and I would be fine for money. But I'd feel like the part of my job that pays is being taken, and the part that matters is left, unpaid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're open to the tools but also want strict rules. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think they clash. I'd use the software for the first draft, but a human with a medical background has to own the final version. If the law says that, there's still work for people like me, just less of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Leon talk about it at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably over breakfast when he's just back from nights and I'm about to go out. He'd say his ward is short of everyone, so why not train as a nurse. I'd laugh, and then I'd lie awake thinking about it.

I'd push the **translators' union** to take that to the health regulator.
think: I think the **trial paperwork**, about two thirds of my income, shifts to cheaper review work.

steps.text: Take a short course in medical translation review software
Ask St Anne's Hospital about a part-time salaried interpreter post
Push the translators' union to lobby the health regulator

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is moving faster than any regulator can, and that's the real scandal. I'd be calling for emergency rules in hospitals and for the companies to fund the people they replace. I'd be loud about it, because I'd have nothing to lose by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think my translation income ends within two years. If a machine can interpret a birth plan as well as I can, the hospital will use it, maybe on a tablet by the bed. The robots coming later don't help, because nothing I do is hands-on. The part of my life that's still safe is Leon's job, at least until 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the nursing access course straight away, since nursing is hands-on and I'd have years before robots catch up. I'd use my savings to cover two years of study, maybe with a student loan on top. I'd cut the extras: no new laptop, no trip, keep the old phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, more than I'd show. And a bit grief-stricken about the language part of me, which I spent ten years building. But also strangely clear, because there would be no time to dither.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why nursing and not something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I already know the wards from interpreting, and Leon has shown me what the work really is, the good and the bad. It uses my Portuguese with patients too. And nursing is one of the few things in this picture where a person still has to touch another person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you worry about you and Leon both being in health jobs that robots reach later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a little. We'd have both our eggs in one basket, as my mum says. But three years is three years, and by then maybe nobody knows anything anyway.

think: I think my **translation income** ends within two years.

steps.text: Apply for the nursing access course at the city college
Cancel the new laptop and the Porto trip
Write to the health minister asking for emergency hospital interpreting rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to get the rules right in health care, so let's use them. I'd push for a law that keeps human interpreters for anything to do with consent and bad news. And I'd say it at the union and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd still earn decent money for maybe two or three of them, while it shrinks. The trial paperwork goes first, then the hospital calls. I'd have time to plan, which matters more than the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working but start the nursing access course part-time in the second year, once the trial work starts drying up. I'd learn the AI tools properly so I can still be useful as a reviewer meanwhile. I'd save a bit more each month, maybe a third of what I earn, as a study fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not frightened. Five years feels like a long goodbye to translation, which is sad. But I'd be making choices, not having them made for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start the course in year one instead of year two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Losing the research company as a client. They're about half my income on their own. If that email came, I'd sign up the same week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep any translation work going alongside nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to, honestly. Even as a nurse I'd be the one on the ward who speaks Portuguese. That's not a job title, but it's useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this well, if we start now. I'd talk about training paths into health care for language workers, paid for by the companies. I'd be calmer and more practical about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years is a whole career stage. I'd translate and interpret until maybe 2032, and still be under forty when I switch. Leon's job holds until robots, which is 2039 in this picture, so we'd have a long runway together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as now and take the AI tools seriously, because they'd keep getting better and I'd want to stay the reviewer people trust. I'd save steadily and maybe buy a small flat with Leon in the next few years. Around 2030 I'd decide between nursing and something else, with real information.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. There's a background worry, like a bill you know is coming. But ten years is long enough that I'd be planning, not reacting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still choose nursing with this much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not. With ten years I could look at things like medical training or health policy, where my languages still count. The fast pictures push me to the quickest safe door, this one lets me look around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger translator starting out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn the tools and pick a field with real people in it, like hospitals or courts. And to keep six months of savings, because savings buy you the right to think.

I'd call for **training paths** into health care for language workers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would force me into nursing whether or not it's right for me. What would help is free or cheap retraining in health care for people like me, and a rule that a human interpreter is there for consent and bad news. Money for study, mostly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the patients. A machine might get the words right, but I've held a woman's hand while her doctor explained a scan. Nobody pays me for that part, and nobody would replace it.

headlineQuote: A machine might get the words right, but I've held a woman's hand while her doctor explained a scan.
portrait: Bianca is a 27-year-old **Portuguese–English** medical translator and on-call hospital interpreter.
She lives with Leon, a **night-shift nurse**, and has over six months saved.
She uses AI **now and then** and wants strict rules so humans sign off medical work.
In the faster pictures she turns to **nursing**, using the three-year gap before robots.
With ten years she'd look more widely at **health careers** that use her languages.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would **force her into nursing** with no time to choose.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **retraining** into health care, and a rule keeping **human interpreters** for consent and bad news.
